transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doc, if you ask my family, they’ll give you a whole song and dance about it. They say I’m here because I went into our savings. But see, they don't see the big picture. I went down to the hardware store—made about five or six trips, actually, loaded up the truck—and I bought wood. I’m talking good, solid plywood, two-by-fours, the works. And lights. I bought every kind of light you can imagine, floodlights, string lights, all this display stuff, the heavy-duty wiring, the outdoor extension cords. 

I had to get it all set up right then and there, you see. So I was out in the yard, building these structures, putting it all together, and I just kept pushing the work after dark. I mean, the sun went down, but the work wasn't done. It was midnight, then 2 AM, 3 AM, and I’m out there hammering and wiring. My wife is hollering from the front door, the neighbors are flicking their porch lights at me and complaining about the noise, but I couldn't just drop my tools. I couldn't. I felt like... well, I just knew, deep down in my gut, that if I stopped working, if I even paused to take a breath or go to bed, the whole house and the entire block would lose its chance. It was all riding on me getting this display finished right then. The opportunity was right there, and I was the only one doing anything about it. But they don't understand that. They just see the bank statement and the yard full of lumber and lights, so they dragged me in here to talk to you.
Did you feel like something bad would happen if you didn't finish the display that night?

Bad? Well, not bad like... like a fire or something, but missed. A missed opportunity of a lifetime! See, I know people think I’m mixed up. My wife, she looks at me like I've got two heads, and the police showing up, they all think it's just some old man making a racket. But they don't get what's actually happening here. I am absolutely sure this neighborhood—our exact street, right there on our block—was picked. Chosen, doc! It was picked for my last big civic art piece. A real, genuine monument for the whole community. 

And I know I'm right. I'm not just making this up, because the proof is right there if you just open your eyes. Little things, you know? Like yesterday, before it got dark and I was out there sorting the two-by-fours, every single vehicle that came down the street—the mail truck, the delivery vans, even just regular pickup trucks—they were all slowing way, way down. Hitting the brakes and just crawling past my driveway. And the neighbors! They were all coming out, leaning over their chain-link fences, pretending to sweep their porches or looking for their cats in the middle of the night, but they were looking right over at my yard. 

It just proves they know it too! They know this is the chosen spot for the art piece, and they were checking on my progress. They were waiting for it to be done. So how could I stop? If I put down my hammer and went to sleep like my wife kept hollering about, I'd be abandoning my duty. The whole project would just be sitting there half-finished when everyone is already watching and waiting for the grand reveal! You don't just walk away from a civic masterpiece when the whole town is driving by to check on it.
Do you feel like you're someone of particular importance or have a special role in the community?

Well, see, importance is a funny word, doc. People hear "important" and they think of mayors or bankers in their suits, you know, the guys with the shiny shoes who talk a big game but don't actually build anything. But me? I'm not some politician. I'm a visionary. That's what they don't get. 

I mean, you look at that old Schiller Park house down the way—just sitting there, peeling paint, looking like a forgotten relic. Everyone else just drives by it, they don't see anything but an eyesore. But I look at it, and I see... I see the potential. I honestly believe I can turn that old house into something important. Something monumental. I can make it into a place that people will travel from all over the county, maybe even the state, just to come see. Because, and this isn't bragging, it's just a fact—nobody, and I mean nobody, understands light and pictures the way I do. 

I've been working with my hands my whole life, sure, but this... this is different. It's about how the shadows hit the wood, how the floodlights can transform a simple piece of plywood into a glowing beacon. It's an art form. And I'm the only one who has the eye for it in this whole town. That's why the neighborhood was chosen, and that's why I'm the one who has to do it. If I don't step up and take on this role, who will? My wife? The guy across the street who can't even mow his lawn straight? No, it has to be me. I have a gift, doc, a real, undeniable gift, and it would be a sin to just let it sit there while I watch TV like some ordinary old man. I'm meant to create this masterpiece.
Do you think you have abilities or powers that most other people do not have?

Well, abilities... powers... I mean, look, I wouldn't call it magic, if that's what you're asking. I'm not pulling rabbits out of hats or flying around like Superman. But yes, absolutely, yes. I have something... an ability, a gift, whatever you want to call it, that these other folks around here just flat out do not possess. 

Like I was saying about that old Schiller Park house, right? You take a hundred people, a thousand people, and you walk them past that place. What do they see? They see a teardown. They see rotten boards and overgrown weeds and maybe a place where teenagers go to drink cheap beer. But me? I look at it, and my brain just works differently. I can already see the finished product. I honestly believe—no, I know—that I can turn that old Schiller Park house into something incredibly important. I'm talking about a real destination, a place where people will load up their cars on a Saturday and drive for hours just to come see what I've done. 

And why? Because nobody... and I mean nobody, not the contractors, not the architects with their fancy college degrees... nobody understands light and pictures the way I do. It's like I have this internal compass for it. I know exactly how a 500-watt halogen bulb is going to cast a shadow against a piece of raw pine at 2:00 AM versus 4:00 AM. I can see the angles before I even pick up a saw. I understand how the visual elements have to flow together to tell a story, to make a real impact on the soul of the person looking at it. It's a deep, profound understanding of illumination and structure. Most people, they just screw in a lightbulb so they don't trip down the stairs. But I use light to create... to create a vision. So yeah, if you want to call that a special ability, then you're darn right I have one. And it's a crime, a real tragedy, that my family wants to lock me in here instead of letting me use it.
Do you always feel like you have this special gift, or is it something that comes and goes?

Well, now, that's... that's a thoughtful question, doc. A very thoughtful question. Because, you see, a man doesn't just wake up every single day of his seventy-three years feeling like he's holding lightning in his hands. It's not like breathing, you know? It's not just always there in the background. 

If I really sit back and think about it—and I have, I've had a lot of time to think sitting in this chair here—before I got so charged up with these remodeling plans, before the vision for the Schiller Park house really took hold of me and demanded to be built... well, I was just going about my business. I wasn't seeing special meaning in the mail trucks driving by, or the delivery vans. I wasn't noticing the way the neighbors were looking at me. I mean, maybe they were looking, maybe they weren't, but it didn't mean anything to me back then. It was just... ordinary life. 

But then, it was like a switch flipped. The ideas started coming, so fast and so clear, and I just felt this incredible drive, this absolute necessity to turn that house into my big civic project. And once that drive hit me, once I felt that surge of purpose, that's when the signs started. That's when I realized the trucks were slowing down on purpose, and the neighbors were checking on my progress. It all clicked together perfectly, but only after the vision took over. So, no, it's not an everyday, all-the-time kind of thing. It's tied to the work. It's tied to the masterpiece. When the inspiration hits, that's when the gift really wakes up and shows me how everything is connected.
Do you feel like you have this special gift all the time, or only when you're working on a specific project like the Schiller Park house?

Well, like I said, it's not an all-the-time thing, no. It's... it's tied to the work, to the vision. And this vision, this specific feeling of having the gift and seeing how everything is connected, it hasn't been forever. It's been... let me think. It's been going on for about three months now. 

Yes, three months exactly. That's when it all started. That's when I got the remodeling started, you see. I decided it was time to finally do something, to stop just sitting around and actually make my mark. So I started tearing things up, getting the materials ready, laying the groundwork for the illumination. And, well, you can imagine, everything in the house got turned upside down. I mean literally upside down. I had extension cords running from the kitchen through the hallway, I had two-by-fours stacked in the living room where my wife usually watches her daytime shows—which she wasn't happy about, let me tell you, but she doesn't see the big picture. 

Anyway, it was right around then, about three months ago, when the house was in absolute chaos, that's when the clarity really hit me. That's when the gift woke up. The more chaotic the house got, the clearer my mind became about the Schiller Park project. It was like I needed to tear down my own normal, boring life to make room for this... this monumental task. So, for the last ninety days or so, day and night, it's been there. The drive, the understanding of the light, the signs from the neighborhood... all of it. Three solid months of pure inspiration, ever since I turned my own house inside out to start the work.
Do you feel as energized and driven as you do now all the time, or are there periods where you feel more subdued?

Subdued? Subdued... no, no, no. That's a word for old men sitting in recliners watching the dust settle and waiting for the clock to run out. That's not me. Not lately, anyway. 

Most days... I'd say nearly every single day since this whole thing started, I wake up and I just feel... charged up. It's this incredible, buzzing energy right in my chest. I feel almost joyful, doc, I really do. It’s like... well, it’s like I’m young again. I’m seventy-three years old, but I swear to you, when I’m working on this, when I’m moving those materials around and seeing the light hit the wood, I have the stamina of a twenty-five-year-old. I don't even want to sit down and rest my joints. I am just humming with this pure, unadulterated joy for the work. 

But... well, I wouldn't say it's all just smiles, because there's a flip side to having this much drive. You see, when you're operating on this level, when you see the masterpiece so clearly in your mind's eye, you expect people to just... get it. Or at least get out of the way. And when they don't... oh boy. If my wife starts in on me—and she does, constantly, nagging about the extension cords, asking me why I'm doing this, telling me to stop—or if those contractors I brought in start questioning my directions... I mean, these guys, they look at my plans and have the nerve to tell me something isn't standard! Standard! They don't understand the vision! 

When they question me, or when my wife questions me, I just... I get hot fast. I mean, zero to a hundred in a split second. The blood just rushes to my face and I start yelling. I can't help it. I yell because they're trying to put a leash on a tiger, you know? They're trying to drag me down to their ordinary, boring little level, and I just won't have it. So yeah, I'm joyful, I'm charged up like a battery, but you cross me on this project, you question what I'm doing, and I will absolutely let you have it.
Do you ever have days where you don't feel as charged up and joyful about your project?

Days where I don't feel charged up? No, no, you're not hearing me, doc. There are no slow days. I mean, I used to be a guy who could sit down and take a load off. I have this old brown recliner, had it for years, right by the front window. Used to sit there for hours just watching the street. But now? I can’t just sit in the chair anymore. I physically cannot do it. If I sit down, it’s like... well, it's like my legs start humming and I just have to get back up immediately. 

I’m up moving all day long. Just constantly in motion, back and forth, back and forth. I'll be out in the garden, pacing out the perimeter, checking the sightlines for how the light is going to hit the foundation, and then two minutes later I'm down in the darkroom—I set up a little photography darkroom in the basement years ago, and it's perfect for reviewing my plans without the glare of the sun distracting me—and then I'm right back upstairs and out on the porch. Garden, darkroom, porch, over and over. 

And I'm carrying tools with me everywhere I go now. I've got pliers in my back pocket, a tape measure clipped to my belt, a screwdriver just tucked into my shirt... always ready for whatever the vision demands. I'm moving so fast I'm fixing things before anyone even asks. My wife will be walking toward the screen door to complain about a loose hinge, and I've already oiled it and tightened the screws while I was mapping out the conduit path across the frame. I just see what needs doing and I do it, boom, boom, boom. So, no, sitting around feeling subdued or un-energized? That just doesn't happen. The work doesn't allow for sitting.
Do you ever have periods where you feel like your energy and joyfulness about the project decrease for a while?

Decrease? No, no, doc, I feel like we’re going in circles here. I keep telling you, it hasn't dropped off for a single second since this whole thing kicked into gear. But... well, I suppose if you mean before all this started, before three months ago? Sure, I guess I was pretty low-energy then. I mean, before I got so completely charged up with these remodeling plans, my life was entirely different. I was just sleepwalking through it. 

I wasn't seeing any of the things I see now. I wasn’t seeing any special meaning in the trucks driving by, for instance. You know, the utility trucks, the delivery vans... they used to just be noise on the street, just regular traffic. I'd sit in that brown recliner I told you about and just watch them roll past, completely blind to what they were doing. And the neighbors, too! I wasn't noticing their looks. Now, when Mrs. Gable across the way waters her petunias and shoots me a glance, I know exactly what she's signaling about the property lines. But before? Nothing. I was totally oblivious to all of it. 

All of those signs, the trucks, the looks from the neighbors... none of that was happening before. Those signs only started once I felt this incredible, undeniable drive to turn the house into my big civic project. Because that's what this is, doc, it’s not just a house remodel, it’s a civic project. It’s for the betterment of the whole Schiller Park area. Once I realized that, once I knew I had to be the one to lay the groundwork and do the illumination for the community, that’s when the universe started communicating with me. The trucks started arriving at exactly the right times to tell me when to measure the conduit, the neighbors started giving me the nods to confirm my sightlines... it all just locked into place. So no, the energy hasn't decreased at all since the civic project began, because the signs just keep coming and telling me I'm exactly where I need to be, doing exactly what I need to do. Why would I slow down when everything around me is telling me to keep going?
Do you ever have times when you feel extremely low or depressed, contrasting with your current high energy and joyfulness?

Depressed? Low? No... no, I wouldn't use those words. Not at all. I mean, look, I told you I was sleepwalking before all this started three months ago, just sitting in that brown recliner watching the dust motes in the sunlight, but that wasn't depression. That was just... a lack of purpose. That was just being an old man who hadn't realized his true calling yet, you know? 

I’ve seen real depression. My old neighbor from years ago, Charlie, now he had that. He wouldn't come out of the house, wouldn't mow his lawn, wouldn't even pick up his newspaper. He just let the weeds grow up past his knees until the city had to come out and fine him. It was a disgrace, honestly. But that was never me. Even when I was just killing time, before the universe woke me up, I always kept the yard neat. I always ate my meals. I never felt that heavy, miserable, crying-in-the-dark feeling people talk about when they talk about being depressed. I was just bored. Waiting, really. Waiting for the signal.

And now? Good lord, doc, how could I possibly be depressed now? I’m too vital! I’m the engine of this whole operation! You think a man who’s tasked with the illumination and betterment of the entire Schiller Park district has time to sit around feeling sorry for himself? I don't even have time to eat a full sandwich most days, let alone sit around moping. If I get low, the whole project stalls. If I stop, the utility trucks keep rolling by and nobody is there to receive the signals. The whole system would just collapse! So no, no depression here. Never had it, certainly don't have it now. I'm just looking forward, always forward, keeping the momentum going. There's just no room for feeling low when you're building something this important.
Do you ever have nights where you feel like you can't sleep because your mind is racing with ideas for your project?

Sleep? Racing mind? Well, doc, it's funny you ask about sleep, because it’s not really about not being able to sleep, you know? It's not like I'm lying there tossing and turning, frustrated because my eyes won't stay shut. It's more like... I just don't need it. I mean, my mind is definitely going, absolutely, 100 percent. It's firing on all cylinders. I'll be in bed, maybe around midnight, and suddenly I’ll see the exact blueprint for the eastern retaining wall just illuminated on the ceiling, clear as day. 

And when you see something like that, a vision that pure and structurally sound, you don't just roll over and try to ignore it. You can't. It would be a crime against the whole Schiller Park district to ignore it! So, I get up. I have to. I'll go down to the kitchen, spread my papers out on the linoleum table—the one with the little chrome edges, you know the kind—and I just start sketching. I'll sketch for hours. Next thing I know, I look out the window over the sink, and the sky is getting that pale, bruised purple color right before the sun comes up. And the crazy thing is, I don't feel tired. Not even a little bit. 

My wife, she'll come down in her robe, rubbing her eyes, telling me I need to come back to bed, that I'm going to run myself into the ground. But she doesn't understand the momentum. She doesn't see the trucks or the signals. If I stop to sleep for eight hours like a regular person, I might miss the exact moment the universe tells me where to lay the main conduit line. So, sure, my mind is full of ideas, bursting with them, but it's not keeping me awake in a bad way. It's fueling me. It's like... it's like I'm plugged directly into the city's power grid, and as long as the ideas are flowing, I don't need to power down. Sleep is just... it's obsolete for me right now. It really is.
Do you ever have days where your enthusiasm and excitement about the project feel less intense than they do now?

Less intense? No, no, it never gets less intense. I'm telling you, most days I just feel so charged up and, well, almost joyful! It’s incredible, really. It’s like I’m young again, back in my twenties with a whole lifetime ahead of me, just buzzing with all this energy and purpose. I haven't felt this alive in fifty years. 

But... well, I guess the feeling itself changes sometimes. Not the intensity, mind you, the intensity is always cranked all the way up. But if someone gets in my way, that joy turns into something else entirely. If my wife comes out and starts questioning me—asking why I'm digging up the driveway at two in the afternoon, or why I'm redirecting the water lines—or if those contractors I hired start dragging their feet and second-guessing my blueprints... oh, buddy, I get hot fast. I mean, my blood just boils right up into my neck and my face, and before I even know what's happening, I start yelling. 

I can't even help it! Just last Tuesday, this guy I brought in to look at the concrete footing, he has the nerve, the absolute gall, to look at my sketches on the kitchen table and tell me my load-bearing calculations don't make sense. Doesn't make sense! After the universe literally handed me the exact dimensions! So I just lost it. I started screaming at him right there in the front yard, told him to get his van out of my sight before I took a crowbar to his windshield. My wife came running out crying, telling me to calm down, which just made me yell louder, because how can I calm down when they're trying to sabotage the work? 

Because, you see, they just don't understand the vision. They want to slow down the whole civic project with their little rules and their tiny little doubts. So no, the enthusiasm doesn't ever drop. I stay fired up from dawn to dusk. But if they push me, if they dare to question what I'm doing for the Schiller Park district, that joyful feeling just ignites into pure fire and I will yell them right off my property. I just don't have the patience for their nonsense, doc, I really don't. We have a neighborhood to illuminate!
Do you ever have periods where you feel like your enthusiasm and excitement about the project are not as high as they are right now?

Well, doc, I feel like we might be going in circles just a little bit here, because like I was just saying, right now? No. The enthusiasm never drops. But if you mean *before* all this started, before the universe tapped me on the shoulder three months ago... well, sure, I guess my enthusiasm was basically zero back then. I was just sitting around. 

But here’s the really important thing you have to understand about that "before" time. Before I got so charged up with all these remodeling plans, I was just a regular, bored old guy. I wasn’t seeing any special meaning in the utility trucks, or in the way the neighbors were looking at me. Three months ago, a white utility truck would roll past the front window, and it was just a truck. I wouldn't even look twice at it, wouldn't even put my coffee down. And the neighbors, like old Mrs. Gable across the street... she’d look over at me getting the mail and it was just a look. Just an old lady being nosy about whether I was going to trim my hedges. I wasn't seeing any special meaning in their looks or the trucks or the way the streetlights flickered at night. None of it. 

All of that... those signs, the signals, the clear messages from the universe... they only started happening once I felt driven to turn this house into my big civic project. It was like a switch got flipped! Once that energy hit me, once I got this incredible, undeniable drive to illuminate and upgrade the Schiller Park district, that's when my eyes were finally opened. That's when I realized the trucks weren't just driving by, they were pacing out the conduit lines for me! And the neighbors were watching because they knew something massive was happening, they could feel the shift in the grid! 

It all clicked together at the exact same time. The energy, the plans, the signs—boom, all at once. I remember the exact day, actually. It was a Tuesday, trash day, and I was just sitting in the recliner, not really enthusiastic about anything, just drinking a cup of lukewarm Folgers. And then the vision for the project hit me like a lightning bolt. And right at that exact second, a city water truck drove by and honked twice. Two honks! The confirmation! Before that day, a honk was just a honk. But since that day? Since the enthusiasm took over and the project began? Every single thing has a purpose. So no, my excitement doesn't drop now. I'm too tuned in. The signals are everywhere, and I've got too much work to do to slow down now.
Do you ever have periods where you feel like your enthusiasm and excitement are not as high as they are right now, even if it's just for a few hours?

Doc, are we... I feel like maybe my hearing aid is acting up, or maybe we're just speaking two different languages here. Because, like I keep trying to tell you, no. Not for a few hours, not for a few minutes, not even for a single second! I just... I don't know why you keep thinking I'm taking breaks or running out of steam. I don't have time to let my excitement drop! 

Think about the logistics of it all, if you really stop to think about it. Just yesterday, for example. Between, let's say, two o'clock and five o'clock in the afternoon. That's three hours, right? If I had just let my enthusiasm wane for those three hours, if I had just sat down in the La-Z-Boy to watch television like some regular retired guy waiting for his pension check, do you know what would have happened? I would have completely missed the surveyor marks. They tied these little yellow ribbons on the telephone pole at the end of the block—pure genius, really, hiding the signals right out in the open—telling me the exact elevation I need for the new drainage pipes I'm mapping out. If I'm sitting around not feeling excited, not paying attention, the whole district floods next spring! 

So, no. I don't have these little dips you keep looking for. My wife, bless her heart, she'll beg me, "Just sit and watch one episode of Wheel of Fortune with me, just for thirty minutes," but I can't! Half an hour of Wheel of Fortune is half an hour the grid goes unmonitored. I don't know how else to say it to you, doc. There are no periods where it drops. The energy is just a constant, rushing river, and I'm steering the ship twenty-four-seven. I don't have time to feel anything less than a hundred percent thrilled about what we're building here.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy or irritable and had a lot of energy, but it wasn't related to your current project?

Unrelated to the project? No, doc, I really... I just don't think you're grasping the timeline of my life here. Before this project? There was no extreme happiness. There was no crazy energy. I was just... I was just a tired old man! 

Look, I left high school in the eleventh grade, right? Went straight to work at the auto body shop over on Elm, and I did that for forty-five years. Banging out dents, sanding primer, breathing in dust day in and day out. By the time I retired, my bones ached and I was just worn out. Ask my wife, she'll tell you! For the last ten years, my whole life was just waking up, reading the paper, maybe getting a little grumpy if the delivery kid threw the Tribune in a puddle, and then taking a nap in my chair by two o'clock. My biggest thrill in a week was going to the hardware store to buy one specific type of wood screw just to kill an hour. That was it! Just a regular, boring, slow existence. 

I never had anything even close to this kind of fire before. I never felt this... this absolute electric charge running through my veins! Why would I? The universe didn't have a mission for me back then. I was just on standby, waiting for the call, even if I didn't know it at the time. So no, I wasn't running around full of energy for no reason back in the day, and I wasn't flying off the handle with irritability unless my sciatica was acting up. 

It’s the project that brought the energy. It’s the Schiller Park district that gave me this incredible joy! You can't separate the two, doc, you just can't. Without the project, I'm just an old guy falling asleep to the evening news. With it? I'm the guy illuminating the whole neighborhood. So no, nothing like this ever happened before the work started. It's all about the work.
Have you ever had a period of time where you felt extremely happy or irritable and had a lot of energy that lasted for at least one week?

A whole week? Doc, I really... I feel like I'm talking to a brick wall here sometimes, no offense. Because I keep saying the exact same thing, and you keep asking it in a slightly different way, like you're trying to catch me in a trap or something. No. Absolutely not. Never a whole week, never a whole weekend, never even a whole afternoon! 

If you're asking if, say, back in 1995, I had a week where I was just bursting with extreme happiness and running around with all this energy... well, my wife would've probably called an ambulance! Because that just wasn't me. You have to understand, a week is a long time when you're spending it sanding down bumpers and inhaling primer fumes at the shop. A whole week of energy? Are you kidding? By Wednesday, my back was killing me. By Friday afternoon, I was practically crawling through the front door just to collapse into my chair. 

There was no extreme happiness lasting a week. What was I going to be extremely happy about? Mowing the lawn on Saturday? Paying the electric bill on Tuesday? Life was just... it was just a flat line, doc. Flat as a pancake. Every single week, fifty-two weeks a year, for my whole life! I never had anything resembling this kind of energy until three months ago when the grid project started. That's the only time I've ever felt this awake, and this has been going on way longer than a week, obviously, because there's so much to do. But before that? Before the universe gave me this purpose? No. Not a chance. I was just a tired guy living a tired life.
Have you ever had a period of feeling extremely low or depressed that lasted for at least one week?

Depressed? For a whole week? No, doc, I don't... I really don't think so. I mean, sure, I've had my moments, like anybody else, right? You live for seventy-three years, you're gonna have some bad days. Like when the shop changed hands back in '08, and the new owner—this kid, couldn't have been more than thirty, wearing a suit to an auto body shop, if you can believe that—he comes in and starts telling us we're using the wrong grade of sandpaper. I was pretty sour about that for a few days, maybe a little down in the dumps, because you pour your heart into a place and then some kid tells you you're doing it wrong. My wife made my favorite meatloaf twice that week just to get me to crack a smile. 

But depressed? Like, really, truly down for a whole week straight? No, no, I wouldn't say that. I was always just too busy, or too tired, to really sit around and wallow. You get up, you go to work, you come home, you eat, you sleep. That was the routine. There wasn't any time to be depressed. And since the project started, well, you know how it is. I haven't had a single second to feel anything but this incredible drive. There's just no room for feeling low when you're the one keeping the whole Schiller Park district from going under. So, no, I can't say I've ever had a week like that. Just the usual bumps in the road, you know?
Have you felt this level of excitement and energy about your project every day since it started?

Every single day, doc. Every. Single. Day. Without fail, without a break, without even a dip in the current! It's like... it's like someone flipped a switch in the breaker box of my brain and just taped it in the "on" position. 

I can tell you exactly when it started, too. It’s been going on for about three months now. Exactly three months. You see, my wife—bless her heart, she means well—she decided the kitchen needed remodeling. After forty years in the house, she suddenly decides the cabinets are too dark and the linoleum is outdated. So, she hires these contractors, and they come in and just completely turn the house upside down. I mean, they tore out the counters, there was dust everywhere—worse than the auto body shop!—and suddenly my whole routine was gone. My chair was moved, the paper was getting delivered to the side door... it was chaos. 

And that's when it happened. Right in the middle of all that remodeling mess, that's when I saw the grid. I realized that the wiring they were exposing in the walls... it wasn't just house wiring.
